question.text:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Remember that an elementary matrix is obtained by performing exactly one elementary row operation on the identity matrix $I.$

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 := R_1 + (-10) R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_1&:= R_1 + (-10) R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= A \end{align*}

  • The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_3 := 7R_3,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_3&:=7R_3 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= B \end{align*}

  • The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_3 := R_3 + (-9)R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_3&:=R_3 + (-9)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= C \end{align*}

Therefore, $A$, $B$, and $C$ are elementary matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Remember that an elementary matrix is obtained by performing exactly one elementary row operation on the identity matrix $I.$

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_3,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_1& \leftrightarrow R_3 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= B \end{align*}

  • The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_3 := R_3 + R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_3&:=R_3+ R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= C \end{align*}

Therefore, only $B$ and $C$ are elementary matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Remember that an elementary matrix is obtained by performing exactly one elementary row operation on the identity matrix $I.$

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2 := R_2 + 2R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_2&:=R_2+2R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= A \end{align*}

  • The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 := R_1 + (-1)R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_1&:=R_1+(-1)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= C \end{align*}

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are elementary matrices.

question.explanation:

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $C$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only $A$ is an elementary matrix.

Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\0 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 10 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Remember that an elementary matrix is obtained by performing exactly one elementary row operation on the identity matrix $I.$

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 := -8R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_1&:= -8R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= A \end{align*}

  • The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2 := R_2 + 10R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} & R_2&:=R_2+10R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 10 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= C \end{align*}

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are elementary matrices.

question.text: Find the inverse of the elementary matrix $ E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
We write down $E$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

\begin{align*} [E\,|\,I \,] & = \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] && R_2 := {\color{blue}-\dfrac 1 3}R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & {\color{blue}-\dfrac 13} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, \[ E^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\dfrac 1 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, \[ B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: Find the product $E_1 E_{2}^{-1}$, where \begin{align*} E_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\qquad E_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
question.explanation:
Notice that $E_1$ and $E_2$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find $E_2^{-1}.$ We write down $E_2$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

\begin{align*} [E_2\,|\,I \,] & = \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] && R_2 := R_2 + (-3)R_3 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ E_2^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we can find the product $E_1 E_{2}^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

\[ E_1 E_{2}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & -11 \end{bmatrix} \]
